title: Karna
body:
Karna

न कुलेन न जात्या वा वीर्यं श्रेष्ठं विभाव्यते।
कर्मणा जायते शूरः पूज्यते सर्वमङ्गले॥

"It is neither by lineage nor by caste that supreme valor is determined. A hero is born of his own actions, and such a soul is worshipped in all auspicious assemblies."

The education of the princes culminated in a magnificent public exhibition of arms in Hastinapur. Arjuna displayed such superhuman archery, utilizing the complex celestial astras, that the vast crowd was lost in absolute wonderment. Suddenly, a sound like rumbling thunder arose from the entrance of the arena. The crowd parted in awed silence to reveal a youth of godlike bearing, from whom natural light and power seemed to emanate. It was Karna, the first-born of Kunti, carrying his innate, celestial armor (Kavacha) and matching golden earrings (Kundala). Unaware of their shared maternal blood, Karna strode up to Arjuna and duplicated every single one of his magnificent feats with effortless, negligent ease.
Duryodhana, thrilled to see a counterweight to Arjuna's prowess, threw his arms around Karna, welcoming him as a brother. But as Karna challenged Arjuna to single combat, Kripacharya intervened, laying down the strict code of the arena: 'Only high-born princes can engage in single combat with a prince of the Kuru line. Reveal, O mighty-armed, your lineage.' Karna's head bent low, like a lotus heavy with rain. Duryodhana immediately stepped forward, declaring: 'If the combat is barred only because he is not a king, I crown Karna as the King of Anga here and now.' Performing the instant consecration with royal waters, Duryodhana invested Karna with the crown and jewels.
Just then, Adhiratha, the old charioteer, tottered into the arena, trembling with fear. Karna, the newly crowned king, immediately knelt and touched the feet of the charioteer in filial reverence, prompting Bhima's cruel, mocking laughter: 'Oh, he is but the son of a suta! Take up the driving whip, you are not worthy of death by Arjuna's arrows.'
Duryodhana's voice cut through the mockery: 'Valor is the hallmark of a Kshatriya; how can you trace great rivers or heroes to their sources? Look at this warrior, his bearing, his armor, and his skill. Can a tiger be born of an antelope? I hold him worthy to rule the entire earth.' Karna's loyalty to Duryodhana was cemented in this moment of defense. Yet, Karna's life remains the most tragic Vedantic study of limiting designations (Upadhis). Born of Surya, his innate armor represents the pristine purity of the soul. But his intense attachment (Kama) to Duryodhana's salt bound his Jivatma to the forces of Adharma. This attachment eventually led him to study under Sage Parasurama by falsely claiming to be a Brahmana. His physical endurance was tested when a stinging worm burrowed deep into his thigh; he remained entirely unmoved lest he disturb his sleeping master. Parasurama, recognizing that only a Kshatriya could bear such physical agony without a tremor, woke in wrath and cursed him: 'Since you deceived your guru, the supreme Brahmastra weapon shall fail you, and the invocatory mantra shall vanish from your memory at your fated hour.'
